task1_delta_alpha.description: Transition width (10%->90% detection) from bootstrap sigmoid k
task1_delta_alpha.interpretation: Transition width median=0.013 (95% CI [0.009, 0.060]). Even the upper CI bound (0.060) is narrower than the alpha_c CI width (0.133), confirming the transition is genuinely sharp despite location uncertainty.

task2_delta_p.description: Detection rate difference p(alpha=0.50) - p(alpha=0.45) from bootstrap sigmoid
task2_delta_p.interpretation: Delta_p median=0.401 (95% CI [0.001, 0.750]). CI lower bound > 0, so detection rates at alpha=0.45 and alpha=0.50 are statistically distinguishable.

task3_fisher.description: Model-free Fisher exact test: alpha=0.45 (0/16) vs alpha=0.50 (18/24)
task3_fisher.interpretation: Fisher exact p=1.48e-06 (highly significant). Rate difference 0.75 (Agresti-Caffo 95% CI [0.475, 0.876]). Model-free confirmation: detection jumps sharply between alpha=0.45 and alpha=0.50.

overall_interpretation: alpha_c CI width (0.133) reflects estimation uncertainty of WHERE the transition boundary sits; Delta_alpha (transition width) is HOW SHARP the transition is. Bootstrap Delta_alpha CI shows the transition is genuinely sharp (narrow Delta_alpha) even though we are uncertain about its exact location (wide alpha_c CI). These are orthogonal quantities: a step function with noisy location estimates would show CI >> Delta_alpha, which is exactly what we observe. Fisher exact test independently confirms the sharp jump (p<1e-6) without any parametric model assumption.
